items.stem: Which species is a radical?
items.answer: CH₃•
items.markingKey: CH₃•. Unpaired electron.

items.stem: Distinguish between an ion and a radical.
items.answer: A radical has an unpaired electron and may be neutral; an ion has a charge from unequal numbers of protons and electrons, usually with all electrons paired.
items.markingKey: A radical has an unpaired electron and may be neutral; an ion has a charge from unequal numbers of protons and electrons, usually with all electrons paired. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the C–F bond in CFCs is not broken in the stratosphere while the C–Cl bond is.
items.answer: The C–F bond (492 kJ mol⁻¹) is much stronger than C–Cl (324 kJ mol⁻¹); the UV photons available have enough energy to break C–Cl but not C–F. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The C–F bond (492 kJ mol⁻¹) is much stronger than C–Cl (324 kJ mol⁻¹); the UV photons available have enough energy to break C–Cl but not C–F. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The bond enthalpy of H–H is 436 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the maximum wavelength of radiation, in nm, that can cause homolytic fission of this bond.
items.answer: 275 nm
items.markingKey: E per bond = 436 × 10³/6.02 × 10²³ = 7.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (M1); λ = hc/E = 2.75 × 10⁻⁷ m (M1) = 275 nm (ultraviolet) (A1).

items.stem: Determine the longest wavelength (nm) of light able to break one C–H bond (bond enthalpy 414 kJ mol⁻¹) and state the region of the spectrum.
items.answer: 289 nm
items.markingKey: A. E per bond = 414 × 10³/6.02 × 10²³ = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (M1); λ = hc/E = 2.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (M1) = 289 nm (ultraviolet) (A1).

items.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes in sunlight. (a) Draw the Lewis structure of H₂O₂. (b) Use the O–O bond enthalpy (144 kJ mol⁻¹) to calculate the maximum wavelength of light that breaks this bond. (c) Show the homolytic fission with fish-hook arrows. (d) Explain why the products are highly reactive.
items.answer: (a) H–O–O–H with two lone pairs on each O. (b) E = 144 000/6.02 × 10²³ = 2.39 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; λ = 8.31 × 10⁻⁷ m (831 nm). (c) H₂O₂ → 2•OH. (d) •OH radicals have an unpaired electron and react rapidly to pair it.
items.markingKey: (a) H–O–O–H with two lone pairs on each O. (b) E = 144 000/6.02 × 10²³ = 2.39 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; λ = 8.31 × 10⁻⁷ m (831 nm). (c) H₂O₂ → 2•OH. (d) •OH radicals have an unpaired electron and react rapidly to pair it.

items.stem: Homolytic fission of a C–Br bond produces
items.answer: two radicals
items.markingKey: B. One electron each.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fish-hook arrow"?
options: A half-headed curly arrow showing the movement of a single electron
The breaking of a covalent bond in which each atom takes one electron of the shared pair, forming two radicals
A species with one or more unpaired electrons
The layer of the atmosphere from about 10 to 50 km above the Earth’s surface, containing the ozone layer
items.answer: A half-headed curly arrow showing the movement of a single electron
items.markingKey: A. "fish-hook arrow" is a half-headed curly arrow showing the movement of a single electron.

items.stem: A student claims: "All radicals carry a charge." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most radicals (Cl•, CH₃•) are neutral; the defining feature is an unpaired electron.
items.markingKey: Most radicals (Cl•, CH₃•) are neutral; the defining feature is an unpaired electron. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does chlorine react with methane in the dark only very slowly?
options: Without UV light, too few Cl–Cl bonds break to start the chain.
items.answer: Without UV light, too few Cl–Cl bonds break to start the chain.
items.markingKey: D. Initiation needs UV.

items.stem: Distinguish between homolytic fission and heterolytic fission.
items.answer: In homolytic fission each atom takes one electron, giving two radicals; in heterolytic fission one atom takes both electrons, giving ions.
items.markingKey: In homolytic fission each atom takes one electron, giving two radicals; in heterolytic fission one atom takes both electrons, giving ions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why homolytic fission usually needs UV light or high temperature.
items.answer: Breaking a covalent bond requires energy equal to the bond enthalpy; UV photons (or high-temperature collisions) supply enough energy per molecule to break the bond evenly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Breaking a covalent bond requires energy equal to the bond enthalpy; UV photons (or high-temperature collisions) supply enough energy per molecule to break the bond evenly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: A radical has an unpaired electron and may be neutral; an ion has a charge from unequal numbers of protons and electrons, usually with all electrons paired.

items.stem: State the products of (a) homolytic and (b) heterolytic fission of the H–Cl bond, and identify which fission gives radicals.
items.answer: (a) H• + Cl•; (b) H⁺ + Cl⁻; homolytic gives radicals
items.markingKey: (a) H• + Cl• (1); (b) H⁺ + Cl⁻ (more electronegative atom takes the pair) (1); homolytic → radicals (1).

items.stem:
The minimum ozone column over Antarctica each October (Dobson units, DU) is shown.

year | minimum ozone / DU
1980 | 320
1985 | 269
1990 | 218
1995 | 166
2000 | 115
2005 | 120
2010 | 130
2015 | 136
2020 | 141

(a) Calculate the mean rate of change of minimum ozone between 1980 and 2000. [2]
(b) Calculate the mean rate of change between 2000 and 2020 and comment on the trend. [2]
(c) Explain why the recovery is much slower than the decline. [2]
(d) Write two equations showing how Cl• catalyses ozone destruction. [2]
items.answer: (a) −10.2 DU per year (b) +1.3 DU per year – slow recovery (c) CFCs already in the atmosphere have lifetimes of 50–100 years and each Cl• destroys many O₃ molecules before termination. (d) Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O• → Cl• + O₂
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (115 − 320)/20 (M1) = −10.2 DU yr⁻¹ (A1). (b) [2] (141 − 115)/20 = 1.3 DU yr⁻¹ (A1); slow recovery after the Montreal Protocol (R1). (c) [2] Long atmospheric lifetimes of CFCs (1); catalytic Cl• (1). (d) [2] Each equation (1 + 1).

items.stem: Using bond enthalpies, which bond, Br–Br, C–Cl, H–H and O=O, can be broken homolytically by the radiation of longest wavelength?
items.answer: Br–Br
items.markingKey: B. Bond enthalpies / kJ mol⁻¹: H–H 436, C–Cl 324, O=O 498, Br–Br 193. Weakest bond needs lowest-energy (longest-λ) photons.

items.stem: Calculate the maximum wavelength of light that can break the Cl–Cl bond (242 kJ mol⁻¹).
Which of Br•, CH₃•, Cl• and OH⁻ is NOT a radical?
items.answer: OH⁻
items.markingKey: D. OH⁻ has all electrons paired.

items.stem: Which of CH₃•, CH₃⁺, CH₄ and H₂O is a radical?
items.answer: CH₃•
items.markingKey: D. CH₃• has an unpaired electron.

items.stem: "Radical reactions are too unselective to be useful in synthesis." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They are less selective than ionic reactions but are industrially and biologically essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: radical halogenation gives mixtures of isomers and polysubstitution; chain reactions are hard to control. Arguments against: radical polymerisation makes poly(ethene) and many plastics; selective radical reactions exist (bromination prefers 3° C–H); radical chemistry is vital in the atmosphere and biology. Supported judgement: They are less selective than ionic reactions but are industrially and biologically essential. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: What is the inorganic product in the propagation steps of methane chlorination?
items.answer: hydrogen chloride
items.markingKey: A. CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl.

items.stem: Mei writes: "In the initiation step, chlorine splits into Cl⁺ and Cl⁻." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: UV light causes homolytic fission into two Cl• radicals.
items.markingKey: UV light causes homolytic fission into two Cl• radicals. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a termination step and a propagation step.
items.answer: A propagation step has one radical on each side (the chain continues); a termination step combines two radicals into a molecule (the chain stops).
items.markingKey: A propagation step has one radical on each side (the chain continues); a termination step combines two radicals into a molecule (the chain stops). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: 2-methylpropane is chlorinated in UV light. How many different monosubstituted isomers are possible?
items.markingKey: C. 2: 1-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (one per distinct hydrogen environment).

items.stem: For the reaction of methane with bromine in ultraviolet light, write equations for the two propagation steps and two termination steps.
items.answer: CH₄ + Br• → CH₃• + HBr; CH₃• + Br₂ → CH₃Br + Br•; Br• + Br• → Br₂; CH₃• + Br• → CH₃Br
items.markingKey: CH₄ + Br• → CH₃• + HBr; CH₃• + Br₂ → CH₃Br + Br•; Br• + Br• → Br₂; CH₃• + Br• → CH₃Br (1 mark per correct equation; radicals shown with •).

items.stem: Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight. (a) Write equations for initiation, two propagation steps and two termination steps. (b) Explain why the reaction is described as a chain reaction. (c) Explain why a mixture of chloromethanes forms and how the yield of CH₃Cl can be increased. (d) Calculate the atom economy for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.
items.answer: (a) Cl₂ → 2Cl•; CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; 2Cl• → Cl₂; CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆. (b) radicals regenerated in propagation. (c) further substitution; use excess CH₄. (d) 50.48/(16.05 + 70.90) × 100 = 58.1 %.
items.markingKey: (a) Cl₂ → 2Cl•; CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•; 2Cl• → Cl₂; CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆. (b) radicals regenerated in propagation. (c) further substitution; use excess CH₄. (d) 50.48/(16.05 + 70.90) × 100 = 58.1 %.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "initiation"?
options: The layer of the atmosphere from about 10 to 50 km above the Earth’s surface, containing the ozone layer
The step in a radical mechanism in which radicals are first formed, e.g. by UV light splitting X₂
Steps in which a radical reacts with a molecule to form a product and another radical, so the chain continues
A compound of carbon, chlorine and fluorine, once used in refrigerants and aerosols, which releases Cl• radicals in the stratosphere
items.answer: The step in a radical mechanism in which radicals are first formed, e.g. by UV light splitting X₂
items.markingKey: B. "initiation" is the step in a radical mechanism in which radicals are first formed, e.g. by UV light splitting X₂.

items.stem: Define the term "radical substitution".
items.answer: A reaction in which a hydrogen atom in an alkane is replaced by a halogen atom via a radical chain mechanism
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reaction in which a hydrogen atom in an alkane is replaced by a halogen atom via a radical chain mechanism. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how dichloromethane can form when methane reacts with chlorine.
items.answer: Chloromethane can itself react with Cl• (CH₃Cl + Cl• → CH₂Cl• + HCl), and CH₂Cl• reacts with Cl₂ to form CH₂Cl₂; excess methane reduces this.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Chloromethane can itself react with Cl• (CH₃Cl + Cl• → CH₂Cl• + HCl), and CH₂Cl• reacts with Cl₂ to form CH₂Cl₂; excess methane reduces this. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: What is the role of UV light in the chlorination of alkanes?
options: It acts as a catalyst for heterolysis.
It breaks Cl–Cl bonds homolytically to start the chain.
items.answer: It breaks Cl–Cl bonds homolytically to start the chain.
items.markingKey: C. Initiation.

items.stem: Why does the reaction of methane with chlorine stop soon after the UV light is switched off?
options: No new radicals are formed and existing ones are removed by termination.
items.answer: No new radicals are formed and existing ones are removed by termination.
items.markingKey: D. Chain ends.

items.stem: Distinguish between a termination step and a propagation step.
items.answer: A propagation step has one radical on each side (the chain continues); a termination step combines two radicals into a molecule (the chain stops).
items.markingKey: A propagation step has one radical on each side (the chain continues); a termination step combines two radicals into a molecule (the chain stops). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why using excess alkane favours the monosubstituted product.
items.answer: Halogen radicals are then much more likely to collide with alkane molecules than with the halogenoalkane product, reducing further substitution.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Halogen radicals are then much more likely to collide with alkane molecules than with the halogenoalkane product, reducing further substitution. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which hydrocarbon is formed in small amounts by a termination step when methane reacts with chlorine in UV light?

items.markingKey: D. CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆.

items.stem: "The ozone hole is caused mainly by carbon dioxide." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The ozone hole is caused by chlorine and bromine compounds (CFCs, halons); CO₂ is linked with global warming, not ozone depletion.

items.stem: Explain the difference between ozone in the troposphere and ozone in the stratosphere.
items.answer: Stratospheric ozone is beneficial, absorbing UV; tropospheric (ground-level) ozone is a harmful pollutant formed in photochemical smog.

items.stem: Explain why HFCs do not deplete ozone even though they reach the stratosphere.
items.answer: They contain no chlorine or bromine; C–F and C–H bonds are too strong to release radicals that catalyse ozone breakdown.

items.markingKey: (a) [2] (104 − 312)/20 (M1) = −10.4 DU yr⁻¹ (A1). (b) [2] (122 − 104)/20 = 0.9 DU yr⁻¹ (A1); slow recovery after the Montreal Protocol (R1). (c) [2] Long atmospheric lifetimes of CFCs (1); catalytic Cl• (1). (d) [2] Each equation (1 + 1).

items.stem: In the stratosphere, O₂ and O₃ absorb UV radiation. (a) Write equations for the photodissociation of O₂ and O₃ and for the formation of O₃. (b) The O=O bond enthalpy is 498 kJ mol⁻¹; calculate the maximum wavelength that can break it. (c) Explain how chlorine radicals disturb this steady state, with equations. (d) Explain why the effect persists for decades.
items.answer: (a) O₂ → 2O•; O₃ → O₂ + O•; O₂ + O• → O₃. (b) E = 8.27 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; λ = 2.40 × 10⁻⁷ m = 240 nm. (c) Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O• → Cl• + O₂ – catalytic, faster breakdown. (d) CFCs have long lifetimes and each Cl• destroys many O₃ molecules before termination.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The Montreal Protocol is the most successful environmental treaty ever."
items.answer: It is a remarkable success, though recovery is slow and replacements created new problems.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: nearly universal ratification; CFC production almost eliminated; ozone layer projected to recover by about 2060; also reduced greenhouse forcing. Arguments against: CFCs persist for decades; recovery is slow; replacement HFCs are powerful greenhouse gases (needed Kigali amendment); illegal emissions have been detected. Supported judgement: It is a remarkable success, though recovery is slow and replacements created new problems. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A half-headed curly arrow showing the movement of a single electron"?
items.answer: fish-hook arrow
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of fish-hook arrow.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Steps in which a radical reacts with a molecule to form a product and another radical, so the chain continues"?
items.answer: propagation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of propagation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A compound of carbon, chlorine and fluorine, once used in refrigerants and aerosols, which releases Cl• radicals in the stratosphere"?
items.answer: chlorofluorocarbon (CFC)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of chlorofluorocarbon (CFC).

items.stem: Why is the hydroxyl radical, •OH, different from the hydroxide ion, OH⁻?
options: •OH has an unpaired electron and no charge; OH⁻ has an extra electron, all paired.
items.answer: •OH has an unpaired electron and no charge; OH⁻ has an extra electron, all paired.
items.markingKey: D. 9 vs 10 electrons.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the propagation steps allow a small amount of UV light to convert a large amount of reactants.
items.answer: Each propagation cycle uses one radical and produces another, so a single initiation can lead to thousands of cycles before termination occurs.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each propagation cycle uses one radical and produces another, so a single initiation can lead to thousands of cycles before termination occurs. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between ozone in the troposphere and ozone in the stratosphere.
items.answer: Stratospheric ozone is beneficial, absorbing UV; tropospheric (ground-level) ozone is a harmful pollutant formed in photochemical smog.
items.markingKey: Stratospheric ozone is beneficial, absorbing UV; tropospheric (ground-level) ozone is a harmful pollutant formed in photochemical smog. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Homolytic fission produces a positive and a negative ion." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: That describes heterolytic fission; homolytic fission produces two radicals.
items.markingKey: That describes heterolytic fission; homolytic fission produces two radicals. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a propagation step and a termination step.
items.answer: A propagation step has one radical on each side (the chain continues); a termination step combines two radicals into a molecule (the chain stops).
items.markingKey: A propagation step has one radical on each side (the chain continues); a termination step combines two radicals into a molecule (the chain stops). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "CFCs damage ozone because they react directly with O₃ molecules." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The CFC must first be split by UV in the stratosphere to release Cl• radicals; it is the Cl• that catalyses O₃ destruction.
items.markingKey: The CFC must first be split by UV in the stratosphere to release Cl• radicals; it is the Cl• that catalyses O₃ destruction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using bond enthalpies, which bond, C–Cl, C–H, H–Cl and O=O, can be broken homolytically by the radiation of longest wavelength?
items.answer: C–Cl
items.markingKey: C. Bond enthalpies / kJ mol⁻¹: O=O 498, C–H 414, C–Cl 324, H–Cl 431. Weakest bond needs lowest-energy (longest-λ) photons.

items.stem: State the number of different monochlorinated products formed from propane and name them.
items.answer: 2: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane
items.markingKey: 2: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane

items.stem: The bond enthalpy for the bond broken in CCl₂F₂ (C–Cl) is 324 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the maximum wavelength of radiation, in nm, that can break this bond.
items.answer: 370 nm

items.stem: The bond enthalpy of H–Cl is 431 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the maximum wavelength of radiation, in nm, that can cause homolytic fission of this bond.
items.answer: 278 nm
items.markingKey: E per bond = 431 × 10³/6.02 × 10²³ = 7.16 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (M1); λ = hc/E = 2.78 × 10⁻⁷ m (M1) = 278 nm (ultraviolet) (A1).

items.stem: For the reaction of methane with chlorine in ultraviolet light, write equations for initiation and the two propagation steps.
items.answer: Cl₂ → 2Cl•; CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
items.markingKey: Cl₂ → 2Cl•; CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (1 mark per correct equation; radicals shown with •).

items.stem: What is the overall equation for the cycle Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O• → Cl• + O₂?
items.answer: O₃ + O• → 2O₂
items.markingKey: A. Add the steps and cancel species on both sides.

items.stem: The bond enthalpy of C–H is 414 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the maximum wavelength of radiation, in nm, that can cause homolytic fission of this bond.
items.answer: 289 nm
items.markingKey: C. E per bond = 414 × 10³/6.02 × 10²³ = 6.88 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (M1); λ = hc/E = 2.89 × 10⁻⁷ m (M1) = 289 nm (ultraviolet) (A1).

items.stem: "Replacing CFCs with HFCs solved the problems caused by CFCs." Discuss.
items.answer: HFCs solved ozone depletion but contributed to climate change, so further replacement is under way.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: HFCs do not deplete ozone; similar useful properties (non-toxic, non-flammable). Arguments against: HFCs are potent greenhouse gases; they are being phased down under the Kigali amendment; alternatives (hydrocarbons, CO₂, HFOs) have other drawbacks. Supported judgement: HFCs solved ozone depletion but contributed to climate change, so further replacement is under way. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Radical reactions are too unselective to be useful in synthesis."
items.answer: They are less selective than ionic reactions but are industrially and biologically essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: radical halogenation gives mixtures of isomers and polysubstitution; chain reactions are hard to control. Arguments against: radical polymerisation makes poly(ethene) and many plastics; selective radical reactions exist (bromination prefers 3° C–H); radical chemistry is vital in the atmosphere and biology. Supported judgement: They are less selective than ionic reactions but are industrially and biologically essential. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "The mechanism of radical substitution is fully supported by evidence." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The radical chain mechanism is well supported by multiple, independent lines of evidence.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: traces of termination products (ethane) are detected; reaction needs UV light and is inhibited by radical scavengers; one photon causes many reactions (chain). Arguments against: individual radicals are hard to observe directly; other mechanisms might also fit some observations. Supported judgement: The radical chain mechanism is well supported by multiple, independent lines of evidence. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "homolytic fission".
items.answer: The breaking of a covalent bond in which each atom takes one electron of the shared pair, forming two radicals
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the breaking of a covalent bond in which each atom takes one electron of the shared pair, forming two radicals. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "termination".
items.answer: Steps in which two radicals combine to form a molecule, removing radicals and ending the chain

items.stem: Which equation represents the natural formation of ozone?
items.answer: O₂ + O• → O₃
items.markingKey: O₂ + O• → O₃. After O₂ photolysis.

items.stem: "All radicals carry a charge." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most radicals (Cl•, CH₃•) are neutral; the defining feature is an unpaired electron.
items.markingKey: Most radicals (Cl•, CH₃•) are neutral; the defining feature is an unpaired electron. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Termination steps are the main source of the product in radical substitution." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most product forms in the propagation steps; termination steps are rare because radical concentrations are low.
items.markingKey: Most product forms in the propagation steps; termination steps are rare because radical concentrations are low. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which statement explains why ozone formation and depletion are in a steady state without pollutants?
options: The rates of ozone formation and breakdown by UV are equal.
Ozone is not affected by UV.
items.answer: The rates of ozone formation and breakdown by UV are equal.
items.markingKey: C. Chapman cycle.

items.stem: Explain why visible light does not split chlorine molecules but UV light does.
items.answer: Each photon’s energy is E = hc/λ; visible photons have too little energy to provide the 242 kJ mol⁻¹ needed per molecule, while shorter-wavelength UV photons have enough.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each photon’s energy is E = hc/λ; visible photons have too little energy to provide the 242 kJ mol⁻¹ needed per molecule, while shorter-wavelength UV photons have enough. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between electrophilic addition and radical substitution.
items.answer: Radical substitution (alkanes + X₂, UV) replaces H with X via radicals; electrophilic addition (alkenes + X₂/HX) adds across C=C via ionic intermediates.
items.markingKey: Radical substitution (alkanes + X₂, UV) replaces H with X via radicals; electrophilic addition (alkenes + X₂/HX) adds across C=C via ionic intermediates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the ozone hole forms mainly over Antarctica in spring.
items.answer: Polar stratospheric clouds form in the extreme winter cold, and reactions on their surfaces convert reservoir compounds into Cl₂; when sunlight returns in spring, Cl₂ photolyses into Cl• that rapidly destroys ozone.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Polar stratospheric clouds form in the extreme winter cold, and reactions on their surfaces convert reservoir compounds into Cl₂; when sunlight returns in spring, Cl₂ photolyses into Cl• that rapidly destroys ozone. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: State the products of (a) homolytic and (b) heterolytic fission of the C–I in CH₃I bond, and identify which fission gives radicals.
items.answer: (a) CH₃• + I•; (b) CH₃⁺ + I⁻; homolytic gives radicals
items.markingKey: (a) CH₃• + I• (1); (b) CH₃⁺ + I⁻ (more electronegative atom takes the pair) (1); homolytic → radicals (1).

items.stem: In the reaction of ethane with chlorine in UV light, which type of step is C₂H₆ + Cl• → C₂H₅• + HCl?
items.answer: propagation
items.markingKey: B. One radical in, one radical out.

items.stem: Which equation shows the first step in the breakdown of chlorotrifluoromethane (CFC-13) in the stratosphere?
items.answer: CClF₃ → CF₃• + Cl•
items.markingKey: D. UV light breaks the weakest bond, C–Cl (324 kJ mol⁻¹), homolytically; C–F (492 kJ mol⁻¹) is not broken.

items.stem: Hexane is chlorinated in UV light. How many different monosubstituted isomers are possible?
items.markingKey: C. 3: 1-, 2- and 3-chlorohexane (one per distinct hydrogen environment).

items.stem: What is the overall equation for the cycle •OH + O₃ → HO₂• + O₂; HO₂• + O₃ → •OH + 2O₂?
items.answer: 2O₃ → 3O₂
items.markingKey: D. Add the steps and cancel species on both sides.

items.answer: Two fish-hook arrows from the bond, one to each Br; Br₂ → 2Br•
items.markingKey: Two fish-hook arrows from the bond, one to each Br; Br₂ → 2Br•
